correctness.rationale: For the repaired RESULT.md, dividing the scalar skew difference by |a|^p+|b|^p reduces its absolute value to the one-variable quotient with u in (0,1), up to endpoint zeros and inversion. With u=exp(−s), stationarity gives cosh((p−1)s)=(p−1)cosh s. The log-derivative of the cosh ratio is (p−1)tanh((p−1)s)−tanh s, with strict sign of p−2 for s>0; the endpoint values give existence and uniqueness on either side of p=2. Equality in the nonnegative pointwise slack therefore forces exactly the indicated signed ratios almost everywhere off the common zero set, and unit normalization forces their |x|^p masses 1/(1+u^p), u^p/(1+u^p). Conversely the two bands make the slack zero. The disjoint-support construction gives two output coefficient lists identical up to permutation and signs, for every τ. Scalar Taylor bounds integrated using Hölder give the uniform O_p(τ^min(p,2)) norm remainders; arithmetic-mean domination supplies the lower bound uniformly even at t=∞ and the balanced pair supplies the common upper bound. Comparing these proves the near-minimizer slack estimate, not a norm-distance claim. The repair explicitly separates the p=2 degeneracy (D_2 identically zero, an orthogonal pair upper bounds all means). Dividing the stationarity residual by p−2 leaves a smooth equation near the Hilbert point; s sinh s−cosh s has derivative s cosh s>0 at its positive root, giving the displayed cusp by the implicit function theorem. Triple and quintuple angles give the stated p=4 and p=6 values. value.rationale: The comparison of a known scalar numerical radius to the geometry of equality in an infinite-dimensional pairwise perturbation is useful beyond the numerical coefficient. Two uniquely located bands, their exact masses, and the near-optimal slack condition provide a reusable diagnostic throughout the non-Hilbert range and for the extreme outer mean, whereas a single attaining two-vector construction or a quartic square identity does not describe that range. The scope is first-order and integrated, not a finite-skew or strong metric stability theorem.
